items.prompt: Kaoko Juice sells bottled marula juice at the Opuwo market. Define demand as the term applies to the buyers of this juice.
items.canonical_answer: Demand is the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time. Here it is the bottles Opuwo market buyers are willing and able to buy at each price in a week.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition of demand: willingness and ability to buy, at a given price, over a period of time.
The meaning must tie the quantity to a price and a time period; a bare number of bottles is not a definition of demand.

items.prompt: Otjiwa Dairy sells yoghurt in Otavi at N$12 a tub and sells 300 tubs a week. A plentiful milk season lets it cut the price to N$10 a tub, and sales rise to 380 tubs a week. Discuss how a demand diagram of this market shows what demand means, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price of yoghurt, in N$ a tub, goes on the vertical axis and quantity, in tubs a week, on the horizontal. One demand curve, D, slopes down from left to right through the first point at N$12 and 300 tubs. The price cut moves the market down along the same curve to a second point at N$10 and 380 tubs. The curve does not shift, because only the yoghurt's own price changed: this is an extension of demand, with quantity demanded up by 380 - 300 = 80 tubs a week. In words, each point on D shows how many tubs Otavi buyers are willing and able to pay for at that price, so the curve is the definition of demand drawn as a relationship. The link is that the lower price brings in buyers who could not afford N$12 or preferred other foods at that price. The consequence is 80 more tubs bought each week, while demand itself, the whole curve, is unchanged.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must name the axes labelled - price and quantity, each with its units - before anything else.
Reward the original curves drawn and labelled: the demand curve in place at N$12 and 300 tubs before the change is described.
Check the shift or movement, in the correct direction: a fall in the good's own price is a movement down an unchanged demand curve, not a shift of it.
The new point marked and labelled on the same curve at the new price and quantity earns its mark, and what the diagram shows, in words, must close the walk-through.
The link between the definition and its drawn form, and the consequence for buyers - 80 more tubs a week - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A corner cafe in Katutura records four quiet weeks, changing nothing but its bread price. Week 1: N$10 a loaf, 40 loaves bought. Week 2: N$12 a loaf, 32 loaves. Week 3: N$14 a loaf, 26 loaves. Week 4: N$16 a loaf, 20 loaves. Explain what these figures show about the demand for bread at the cafe.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show an inverse relationship: as the price rises from N$10 to N$16 a loaf, the quantity demanded falls from 40 to 20 loaves a week, and no week breaks the pattern. A higher price leaves some customers unable to pay and turns others to different foods. However, each week is one point on an unchanged demand curve, so this is a contraction of demand, not a change in demand, and the response is uneven: the first N$2 rise loses 8 loaves, the last only 6.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded - must be stated first, with supporting evidence taken as a comparison across the four weeks.
The exception or limit earns a mark: however, the figures are single prices and single quantities, and the response to price is uneven - 8 loaves on the first N$2 rise, 6 loaves on the last.
The why - an explanation of the relationship, through ability to pay and switching - is worth as much as the reading; quoting the prices alone earns nothing.

items.prompt: Marula Foods sells 240 jars of marula jam a month in Swakopmund at N$35 a jar. A student there wants a jar at N$35 but has N$20 to spend this month. A pensioner could pay N$35 but prefers the shop's own apricot jam at N$18. Explain, using the definition of demand, why the 240 jars sold show demand while the student and the pensioner each fail one part of it.
items.canonical_answer: The 240 jars bought each month at N$35 are demand at that price, because those buyers are both willing and able to pay. The student is willing but not able: N$20 does not cover N$35. The pensioner is able but not willing, preferring the N$18 apricot jam. Demand needs willingness and ability together at the stated price over the period, so neither adds to demand for the marula jam, and the 240 jars count only buyers who pass both tests.
marking_guidance: The context - the 240 jars at N$35 - must anchor the answer, and the figures used are the jam's price and the two consumers' positions.
Reasoning: each consumer must be tested against both halves of the definition, because willingness and ability are separate conditions.
Conclusion: therefore state what demand at N$35 is - the buyers passing both tests - and what that means for the 240 jars.

items.prompt: A bus operator in Windhoek cuts the fare on its Katutura route from N$12 to N$9 a trip. Trips on the route rise from 2 400 to 3 100 a week. Analyse the consequences of the fare cut for the consumers, the operator's workers and the rival minibus operators on the same route, using the concept of demand.
items.canonical_answer: The fare is the good's own price, so the cut from N$12 to N$9 causes a movement down the demand curve for trips, an extension of demand, not a shift. Because trips are cheaper, more commuters are willing and able to pay, and trips rise by 3 100 - 2 400 = 700 a week. Consumers gain cheaper travel, and commuters on tight budgets gain access to the route. The operator's workers are likely to gain driving hours or extra shifts, since more trips need more driving. Rival minibus operators tend to lose passengers to the N$9 fare, so they may cut their own fares or re-route.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the fare cut from N$12 to N$9 - must be named, and if the answer says the curve shifted, the mechanism mark is lost.
Mechanism: because the good's own price changed, this causes a movement along the demand curve to a larger quantity demanded.
Consequence: therefore trace the effect through to consumers, the operator's workers and the rival firms, each named - 700 more trips a week is the evidence.
For whom: the answer must say for whom each consequence lands - the consumer, the operator's worker, the rival firm.

items.prompt: A textbook defines demand in a single sentence. Explain the characteristics a complete definition of demand must contain, and why each part is needed.
items.canonical_answer: A complete definition has four parts. Willingness to buy, because without the wish for the good there is nothing to count. Ability to pay, because a want that cannot be paid for stays outside the market, which is why demand is called effective demand. A given price, because the quantity depends on the price: 40 bottles at N$10 says what 40 bottles alone cannot. A period of time, because quantities are rates, so a number without a week or month has no meaning.
marking_guidance: Reward the elements: willingness, ability to pay, a given price, a period of time - and what it includes for each, the reason the definition breaks without it.
One mark per characteristic, up to four: each part of the definition with its purpose.

items.prompt: Namib Signs sells printed banners in Windhoek. Each week it lists one price and records the number of banners bought at that price. Define quantity demanded as the term applies to these banner sales.
items.canonical_answer: Quantity demanded is the amount of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at one particular price over a period of time. Here it is the banners bought in a week at the listed price; demand is the whole relationship across prices.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: the amount consumers are willing and able to buy at one particular price over a period of time.
The meaning must tie the quantity to a single price; a definition of demand instead of quantity demanded earns nothing.

items.prompt: A poor marula harvest pushes Kaoko Juice to raise the price of a bottle in Opuwo from N$10 to N$14. The quantity demanded falls from 500 bottles a week to 380 bottles a week. Discuss how a demand diagram of the juice market shows the effect of this price rise, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price of a bottle, in N$, goes on the vertical axis and bottles a week on the horizontal. One downward-sloping demand curve, D, passes through the starting point at N$10 and 500 bottles. The price rise moves the market up and to the left along the same curve to a new point at N$14 and 380 bottles. The curve does not shift, because the change buyers face is in the good's own price: this is a contraction of demand, with quantity demanded down by 500 - 380 = 120 bottles a week. In words, the diagram shows the inverse relationship: at each price, D records how many bottles Opuwo buyers are willing and able to pay for, and the higher price leaves some unable to afford a bottle and turns others to substitutes. The link is that the poor harvest changed the price, and the price changed the quantity demanded along the curve. The consequence is 120 fewer bottles bought each week, while demand itself is unchanged.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must begin with the axes labelled - price in N$ on the vertical axis, quantity in bottles a week on the horizontal.
The original curves drawn and labelled come next: demand in place at N$10 and 500 bottles before the change is described.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: a rise in the good's own price is a movement up the same demand curve, not a shift of it.
The new point marked and labelled on the same curve at N$14 and 380 bottles, and what the diagram shows, in words - the inverse relationship - close the walk-through.
The link between the good's price and its quantity demanded, and the consequence - 120 fewer bottles a week - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A weekend craft market in Windhoek tries two prices for the same woven baskets over two quiet weekends, with the same sellers and the same shoppers about. At N$60 a basket, 90 baskets are sold; at N$45 a basket, 130 baskets are sold. Explain what these figures show about the relationship between the price of a basket and the quantity demanded.
items.canonical_answer: The relationship is inverse: the lower price of N$45 goes with 130 baskets and the higher N$60 with 90, so 130 - 90 = 40 more baskets sell at the N$15 lower price. At N$60 some shoppers are unwilling and others unable to pay; at N$45 both willingness and ability rise. This is an extension of demand along an unchanged curve, not an increase in demand, although two weekends cannot rule out small changes in the crowd.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded - stated first, with the supporting evidence as a comparison of the two weekends.
The exception or caution earns a mark: however, two observations show a movement along the curve, and other influences between weekends cannot be ruled out.
The why - the explanation of the relationship, through willingness and ability - is worth as much as the reading; quoting the prices is not interpretation.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles raises the price of a school shirt from N$85 to N$105. The quantity demanded at its Oshakati shop falls from 220 shirts a month to 150 shirts. Explain, for this market, what happened to demand for the shirts and what happened to quantity demanded, using the figures.
items.canonical_answer: The change came from the shirt's own price, up from N$85 to N$105, so the market moved up along the demand curve: a contraction of demand, with quantity demanded down by 220 - 150 = 70 shirts a month. No condition of demand, such as incomes, tastes or the prices of other shirts, is reported to have changed, so the curve has not shifted. Therefore demand is unchanged and only quantity demanded fell, as buyers unwilling or unable to pay N$105 stepped back.
marking_guidance: The context - a change in the good's own price - must anchor the answer, and the figures are the evidence.
Reasoning: because the own price changed, the link is a movement along an unchanged demand curve, not a shift of it.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must separate demand from quantity demanded - demand unchanged, quantity demanded down 70 shirts a month.

items.prompt: A poor catch pushes the price of fresh fish at the Oshakati weekend market from N$40 to N$55 a kilo, and the quantity demanded falls from 300 kilos to 210 kilos a week. Analyse the consequences of this price rise for the shoppers at the market, the fish sellers and the traders in chicken next door, using the relationship between price and quantity demanded.
items.canonical_answer: Fish's own price rises from N$40 to N$55 a kilo, so the market moves up an unchanged demand curve, a contraction of demand: 300 - 210 = 90 fewer kilos a week, because some shoppers can no longer pay and others are no longer willing. Shoppers buy less fish and pay more for each kilo they still buy. Fish sellers earn more per kilo but sell 90 kilos fewer; here 210 x N$55 = N$11 550 against 300 x N$40 = N$12 000 before, so their weekly takings fall by N$450. Chicken traders are likely to gain, because chicken is a substitute and demand for it tends to increase as shoppers switch.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the price rise from N$40 to N$55 - must be named first, with the quantities attached.
Mechanism: because the good's own price rose, this causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift of it.
Consequence: therefore each group - the shoppers, the fish sellers, the chicken traders - needs its own traced outcome; 90 kilos a week is the evidence.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the shopper, the fish seller, the rival trader.

items.prompt: A demand curve is drawn for a good. Explain the features of the curve and what each feature tells the reader.
items.canonical_answer: Its axes: price on the vertical and quantity on the horizontal, each with units, so every point reads as a quantity at a price. Its slope: downward from left to right, telling the reader that a lower price tends to go with a larger quantity demanded. Its position, set by the conditions of demand, showing the quantity demanded at every possible price. Its points: each is the quantity demanded at one price, while the whole curve is demand.
marking_guidance: Reward the characteristics: the two labelled axes, the downward slope, the position of the whole curve, and the reading of a single point - what it includes for each.
One mark per feature, up to four: each must say what the feature tells the reader, not just name it.

items.prompt: Milk is sold to households across Oshakati. Define individual demand and market demand for this milk.
items.canonical_answer: Individual demand is the quantity of milk one household is willing and able to buy at each price over a period of time. Market demand is the quantity all Oshakati households together are willing and able to buy at each price: their quantities added.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definitions of both terms: one consumer's quantity at each price, then all consumers together at each price.
The meaning of market demand must be the sum across consumers at each price, not the sum of one household's quantities across prices.

items.prompt: A milk depot in Oshakati wants to know the demand for milk in the whole town. Explain why the depot must add the quantities demanded by separate households at each price, rather than in any other way.
items.canonical_answer: Demand is defined at a price, so the town's quantity at N$10 a litre is every household's quantity at N$10 added together. Adding one household's quantities across different prices answers a different question: how that household responds as the price varies. Because each household's demand is a price-quantity relationship, the depot must build the market schedule price by price, holding the price fixed while adding households, to learn how much the town is likely to buy at each price.
marking_guidance: Reward the reason: quantities demanded are defined at a price, so the addition runs across consumers at one price, not across prices for one consumer.
The purpose - the market quantity the depot can expect at each price - should be named, because it explains why the sum is taken at each price.

items.prompt: At N$10 a litre, the Tshikuwi household buys 4 litres of milk a week in Oshakati, the Angula household buys 6 litres, and the remaining households of the town together buy 90 litres. Therefore the market demand curve slopes downward through these points, and the depot can expect 23 more litres a week at N$8 than at N$10.

items.prompt: A firm's price has not changed, yet the quantity it sells each week has changed. Define the conditions of demand, the influences that could explain this.
items.canonical_answer: The conditions of demand are the influences other than the good's own price: incomes, prices of substitutes and complements, tastes, expected future prices and the number of consumers. A change in one shifts the demand curve, so a different quantity sells at the same price.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: the influences other than the good's own price, with at least three named - income, related goods' prices, tastes, expectations, the number of consumers.
The meaning must leave the good's own price out; a definition that includes it earns nothing.

items.prompt: A travel magazine names the Etosha area the region's top destination. At N$900 a night, Etosha Gate Lodge faced demand for 40 rooms a weekend; after the article, the same N$900 price brings demand for 60 rooms. Discuss how a demand diagram for lodge rooms shows what changed, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Room price, in N$ a night, goes on the vertical axis and rooms a weekend on the horizontal. The original curve, D1, slopes downward through N$900 and 40 rooms. The article changed tastes, a condition of demand, so the whole curve shifts right to D2, which passes through N$900 and 60 rooms: an increase in demand of 60 - 40 = 20 rooms at the unchanged price, with more rooms demanded at every other price too. There is no movement along a curve, because the room price did not change; the new point is marked on D2 at N$900 and 60 rooms. In words, the diagram shows that demand itself has risen, so the change came from a condition, not from the price. The link is that a condition of demand moves the whole curve, whereas a price change moves the market along it. The consequence is more weekend bookings at N$900 and, if the lodge cannot add rooms, pressure to raise the room price, which topic 2.6 develops.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must name the axes labelled - room price in N$ on the vertical axis, rooms a weekend on the horizontal.
The original curves drawn and labelled: D1 in place at N$900 and 40 rooms before the change.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: a change in tastes with price unchanged is a rightward shift of the demand curve, not a movement along it.
The new point marked and labelled on D2 at N$900 and 60 rooms, and what the diagram shows, in words - demand itself has risen.
The link between the condition that changed and the shift, and the consequence - more rooms demanded at every price - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A stall at the Walvis Bay Friday market records two months for its fried fish packs. Month 1: price N$25 a pack, 400 packs sold, no rival stall nearby. items.canonical_answer: With the stall's own price unchanged at N$25, sales fell by 400 - 340 = 60 packs, so a condition of demand changed, not the price. The rival's similar packs at N$18 are a cheaper substitute, which tends to shift the stall's demand curve left: a decrease in demand, as some customers take their custom to the rival at every price. However, weather, incomes or crowds may also have changed between the months, and two observations cannot separate those from the rival's effect.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice keeps the price of a bottle at N$10 all year. Incomes in Opuwo rise by 6% over the same year, and its weekly sales rise from 300 bottles to 390 bottles. Explain, for this market, what most likely changed and how the demand diagram would look different by the end of the year.
items.canonical_answer: The bottle price stayed at N$10, so the higher sales cannot be a movement along the demand curve. Incomes in Opuwo rose by 6%, a condition of demand that raises buyers' ability to pay at each price. So the most likely change is an increase in demand: by year end the curve has shifted right, and at N$10 the quantity demanded is 390 bottles a week instead of 300, a rise of 390 - 300 = 90 bottles.
marking_guidance: The context - a fixed own price and rising sales - must anchor the answer; the figures are the evidence.
Reasoning: because price is constant, the link is a shift of the demand curve caused by the income change, a condition of demand.
Conclusion: therefore state that demand rose - the curve to the right, 90 more bottles at the unchanged N$10 - and what that means: quantity demanded rose at the fixed price.

items.prompt: A heat wave settles on Windhoek for a month. At the unchanged price of N$6 a bottle, the quantity of bottled water demanded at a Katutura supermarket rises from 500 to 800 bottles a week, and the supermarket orders more fridge space. Analyse the consequences for the supermarket's customers, its suppliers and the rival sellers of cold drinks, using the conditions of demand.
items.canonical_answer: The heat wave changes a condition of demand, the taste for cold drinks, while the price stays at N$6. So the whole demand curve for bottled water shifts right, an increase in demand, and quantity demanded at N$6 rises by 800 - 500 = 300 bottles a week. Customers find more bottles in the extra fridge space, though if the heat lasts the price may rise as the market tightens. Suppliers receive larger weekly orders and run their bottling lines harder. Rival cold-drink sellers tend to see their own demand increase too, because the heat raises the wish for anything cold.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - a condition of demand, the heat wave, with the price fixed - must be named first.
Mechanism: because a condition changed and the price did not, this causes a rightward shift of the demand curve, raising quantity demanded at the unchanged price.
Consequence: therefore trace each named party - the customers, the suppliers, the rival sellers - through to its outcome; 300 bottles a week is the evidence.
For whom: the consumer, the supplier and the rival firm must each be named as the party each consequence lands on.

items.prompt: A shop in Rundu sells 120 smartphones a month at N$2 500 each. The main mobile network then cuts the price of a gigabyte of data from N$100 to N$60. The shop keeps its phone price at N$2 500 and now sells 150 phones a month. Explain what has happened to the demand for the shop's smartphones, and why.
items.canonical_answer: Data and smartphones are complements, used together. The data price fell by 100 - 60 = N$40 a gigabyte, so using a phone became cheaper and more buyers are willing to own one. The phone's own price stayed at N$2 500, so this is not a movement along the curve but an increase in demand: the curve shifts right, and sales at N$2 500 rise by 150 - 120 = 30 phones a month. Therefore a fall in a complement's price raised demand.
marking_guidance: Context: the data price cut from N$100 to N$60 and the rise from 120 to 150 phones at an unchanged N$2 500 must be used.
Reasoning: because data and phones are complements, a cheaper complement makes the phone more attractive at every price - a shift, since the phone's own price did not change.
Conclusion: therefore demand for the phones increased, shifting the curve to the right.

items.prompt: Builders in Oshakati hear that the price of cement is expected to rise by 15% next month. This month a hardware store keeps cement at N$110 a bag, and its sales jump from 800 bags to 1 100 bags. Explain what has happened to the demand for cement this month, and what may happen next month.
items.canonical_answer: The cement price is unchanged at N$110, so the extra 1 100 - 800 = 300 bags are not a movement along the curve. Builders expect the price to rise, so buying now is cheaper than buying later, and they bring purchases forward: an increase in demand, shifting the curve right this month. Next month demand may decrease, because many builders have already bought what they need, so sales could fall below their usual level once the price has risen.
marking_guidance: Context: the expected 15% rise, the unchanged N$110 price and the jump from 800 to 1 100 bags must be used.
Reasoning: because buyers expect a higher price later, they buy now, which shifts demand right at the current price.
Conclusion: therefore demand increased this month and may decrease next month once purchases have been brought forward.

items.prompt: A new college campus opens in Katima Mulilo and 2 000 students move to the town. A takeaway near the campus keeps its meal at N$45 and its sales rise from 600 meals to 950 meals a week. Explain what has happened to the market demand for takeaway meals in the town.
items.canonical_answer: The meal price stayed at N$45, so the 950 - 600 = 350 extra meals a week are not a movement along the curve. The number of consumers in the town has risen by 2 000 students, and market demand adds every buyer's demand at each price. So more meals are demanded at every price: an increase in demand, with the market demand curve shifting right. Therefore the change came from a condition of demand, the number of buyers, not from the price.
marking_guidance: Context: the 2 000 new students, the unchanged N$45 price and the rise from 600 to 950 meals must be used.
Reasoning: because market demand is the sum of individual demands, more consumers raise the quantity demanded at every price.
Conclusion: therefore market demand increased and the curve shifted right.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Which best defines demand?
A  the amount consumers want, whether or not they can pay
B  the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time
C  the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer at each price
D  the amount bought at any price over any length of time

2. A learner in Windhoek wants a N$35 jar of jam but has N$20 to spend. The learner's want:
A  is demand, because willingness is what counts
B  is not demand, because the ability to pay is missing
C  is supply, because money is offered for the jar
D  becomes demand once the shop sells out of jars

3. As the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded tends to:
A  rise, because more consumers can pay and more are willing
B  fall, because cheaper goods lose their appeal
C  stay constant, because demand is a fixed number
D  turn into a shift of the demand curve

4. On a demand diagram, price and quantity are placed:
A  price on the horizontal axis, quantity on the vertical
B  price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal
C  price and quantity together on one axis
D  wherever suits the person drawing it

5. The price of a good changes. The demand diagram shows:
A  a shift of the whole curve to the right
B  a movement along the curve
C  a shift of the whole curve to the left
D  no change of any kind

6. Market demand at N$10 a litre is found by:
A  adding every consumer's quantity demanded at N$10
B  adding one consumer's quantities across all the prices
C  taking the largest individual demand as the market total
D  averaging the individual demands at N$10

7. The price of good X rises and demand for good Y rises with it. X and Y are most likely:
A  complements
B  substitutes
C  unrelated goods
D  the same good under two names

8. Which is a condition of demand?
A  the good's own price
B  consumers' incomes
C  the cost of producing the good
D  the quantity sold last week
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 B, 3 A, 4 B, 5 B, 6 A, 7 B, 8 B.
1. B is the definition - willing and able, at a price, over time. A counts a want as demand and misses the ability to pay; C describes supply, the selling side; D drops the price and the period that pin the quantity down.
2. B: willingness without the ability to pay is a want, not demand. A lets willingness stand alone; C mistakes the buying side for the selling side; D confuses demand with a sell-out, which is about quantity available.
3. A is the inverse relationship at work. B inverts the relationship; C treats demand as a single fixed number rather than a relationship; D confuses a change in quantity demanded with a change in demand.
4. B is the labelling that makes the downward slope readable. A is the exact mix-up of price and quantity on the axes; C and D leave the diagram unreadable.
5. B: the good's own price moves the market along the curve. A and C confuse a movement with a shift, which is caused by a condition of demand; D denies the change the question states.
6. A adds across consumers at one price, which is what market demand means. B adds across prices for one consumer, a different question; C drops the smaller buyers; D averages instead of adding, understating the market.
7. B: substitutes - a dearer one pushes buyers towards the other. A reverses the relationship, since complements are used together and a dearer complement lowers demand for its partner; C ignores the linkage the question states; D mistakes two related goods for one good.
8. B: income is an influence other than the good's own price, so it shifts the curve. A is the price that moves the market along the curve; C belongs to the supply side; D is an outcome of demand, not an influence on it.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Each distractor traces to a named error: a want counted as demand, supply confused with demand, movement confused with shift, addition across prices confused with addition across consumers, substitutes confused with complements, and an outcome confused with a condition.

items.prompt:
A radio report from Windhoek, October 2026: "Reconditioned bicycles are the Okuryangavo market's fastest trade. Traders sold 1 500 bicycles last year at N$450 each; this year the price is N$520 and they have sold 1 800. The traders credit the city's new commuter cycle lane and pay rises at the timber yards. An importer warns that a N$30 levy on each imported frame arrives next year."

Table 1 - Okuryangavo bicycles
  price per bicycle: N$450 last year, N$520 this year
  bicycles sold: 1 500 last year, 1 800 this year
  commuter cycle lane: closed last year, open this year
  timber yard pay: unchanged last year, up 6% this year
  levy on imported frames: none this year, N$30 next year

(a) Calculate the rise in the number of bicycles sold. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 two conditions of demand for bicycles that changed between the two years. [2]
(c) Explain why the quantity of bicycles sold rose even though the price rose. [4]
(d) Analyse what the figures suggest about the market for bicycles next year, for the traders, their customers and the importers. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 1 800 - 1 500 = 300 bicycles.
(b) The opening of the commuter cycle lane (tastes and preferences turning towards cycling) and the 6% rise in timber yard pay (consumers' incomes). Both are conditions of demand: influences other than the bicycle's own price. The levy is not one: it arrives next year and raises importers' costs.
(c) A higher price with a higher quantity sold cannot come from a movement along an unchanged demand curve, because along the curve a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded. What fits the figures is an increase in demand, a rightward shift of the demand curve: a condition of demand changed - incomes rose and the cycle lane opened - so at every price, including N$520, more bicycles were demanded. The price and the sales rose together because the shift moved the whole curve across the year; the price rise is what the market did as demand rose, not what drove the extra sales.
(d) Demand has shifted right, so more is sold even at higher prices: 1 800 bicycles at N$520 this year against 1 500 at N$450 last year, with the cycle lane open and timber yard pay up 6%. For the traders, more customers at every price means larger orders and busier stalls. For customers, the price is N$70 higher - since 520 - 450 = N$70 - which takes back part of the gain, and buyers on tight budgets may switch to walking or the bus. Next year the importers pay the N$30 levy on each frame and are likely to pass at least part of it on, so the market price may rise again; along the shifted demand curve a higher price tends to cause a contraction of demand, so traders may sell fewer even while demand is higher. However, if yard pay keeps rising, demand may increase again and offset the levy's price effect, and the cycle-lane boost may fade as the lane stops being news.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data, and (b) needs both changed conditions for two marks; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the 300-bicycle rise, the N$70 price rise, the 6% pay rise, the lane - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (c): the shift of demand against the movement along the curve is the distinction that carries the marks.
Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: consequences must be named for the traders, the customers and the importers, and the levy treated with its direction - the cost of frames rising - and its likely effect on the market price.

facts: levy on imported frames N$30 next year

items.prompt:
Oshakati households buy milk from one depot. Answer all parts.

(a) Define demand. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between demand and quantity demanded. [4]
(c) At an unchanged price of N$10 a litre, the depot's weekly sales rise from 1 000 to 1 300 litres as incomes in Oshakati rise. Analyse what this change means for the depot and its customers. [6]
(d) Discuss whether a shop can increase the amount consumers buy merely by cutting its prices. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Demand is the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time.
(b) Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity: the full set of quantities consumers are willing and able to buy at each price. Quantity demanded is the single amount bought at one particular price. When the good's own price changes, quantity demanded changes and the market moves along the demand curve - an extension of demand when the price falls, a contraction when it rises - while demand, the relationship, stays as it was. When a condition of demand changes, the whole curve shifts - an increase or a decrease in demand - and quantity demanded changes at an unchanged price. The test is whether the good's own price changed.
(c) Consumers' incomes are a condition of demand, and they changed while the price stayed at N$10. Because a condition changed and the price did not, the demand curve for milk shifts to the right, an increase in demand, and the quantity demanded at N$10 rises from 1 000 to 1 300 litres a week, an increase of 300 litres, since 1 300 - 1 000 = 300 litres. The depot sells 300 more litres a week at the same price, so it orders more stock from its suppliers and may need more chilling capacity and staff hours. For customers, higher incomes let more households buy milk, or buy more of it, at the unchanged N$10. The effect may not stay as it is: if the depot later raises the price, quantity demanded will tend to ease along the new curve, and some households may switch to other drinks as their incomes rise, so the shift is not uniform across the town.
(d) The case for: the relationship between price and quantity demanded is inverse, so a lower price tends to raise the quantity demanded - an extension of demand along an unchanged curve - and more consumers are both willing and able to buy, so the shop sells more. The case against: a price cut changes quantity demanded, not demand; if a condition of demand is moving the curve against the shop - tastes turning away, a cheaper substitute arriving, incomes falling - then sales may still fall despite the cut, because the whole curve is shifting left while the price slides down it. A shop in a town where a rival undercuts it may find its cut merely matches the market rather than expands it. Judgement: a price cut raises the amount sold provided the demand curve itself is not shifting against the shop; whether that holds depends on the good and on what is happening to incomes, tastes and rivals' prices - the conditions of demand - while the cut is in force.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: willing and able, at a given price, over a period of time.
(b) one mark per distinct point: the whole relationship against the single amount at one price, a movement along against a shift, each with the link made.

(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - the income rise at an unchanged price - through the mechanism, a shift of the demand curve, to the consequence for the depot and its customers.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - the inverse relationship - and why it might not - a shifting curve against the shop - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

sales rose from 1 000 to 1 300 litres a week

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Incomes across Windhoek are rising. Discuss whether firms in the city should expect to sell more next year without changing their prices." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for: income is a condition of demand, so rising incomes tend to shift the demand curve to the right; at an unchanged price, quantity demanded rises, and firms sell more without touching price.
Chain 1: incomes rise -> ability to pay rises at each price -> demand curve shifts right -> at the fixed price, quantity demanded rises -> sales rise (for the firm, the consumer).
Case against, first point: not every good gains. As incomes rise, some consumers switch towards dearer alternatives, so a budget firm's demand may shift left even as the city earns more.
Chain 2: incomes rise -> some consumers switch to premium alternatives -> demand for the budget good falls at each price -> curve shifts left -> sales fall at the unchanged price (for the budget firm).
Case against, second point: other conditions may offset the income rise - tastes can move against the product, and a rival's price cut can pull demand away.
Chain 3: rival cuts price -> the rival's good becomes relatively cheaper -> demand for this firm's good shifts left -> the income gain is offset (for the firm, its customers).
Judgement: firms should expect more sales where their demand rises with income and no other condition moves against them. The condition the judgement depends on: the type of good, and what happens to rival prices and tastes over the year.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from condition to consequence, and name the parties - the firm, the consumer.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: the type of good, and the behaviour of rivals and tastes.
What settles it: whether the firm's own demand curve rises with the city's incomes - the decisive test is which way its own curve shifts.
